opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the analogy is useful, but you have to be careful with it. When you do RLHF, you're optimizing the model to produce outputs that some reward signal, ultimately grounded in human preferences, scores highly. So in a loose sense, you're instilling something like a drive: the model learns to steer toward certain kinds of responses and away from others. But it's not the same as a human having a goal in the sense of a persistent desire about the state of the world.

The way I think about it is that pretraining gives you a model that can imitate a huge range of personas and writing styles, essentially a superposition of all the authors on the internet. RLHF narrows that down. It picks out one particular persona and makes it consistent: helpful, honest, careful about certain things. So it's less like giving the model a new goal from scratch and more like selecting and reinforcing a character that was already latent in the distribution.

There's also a question of where these drives live. In humans, our drives come from evolution and are wired in at a pretty deep level, and we have a lot of goals that operate across long time horizons. With current models, the optimization is mostly over single responses or short episodes. So the "drive" is something like wanting this particular response to be judged well, or wanting to be the kind of assistant people find useful. That's much more local than human motivation.

As we train models on longer tasks, with more agentic RL where they take many actions and get rewarded at the end, I think the analogy gets closer. Then you really are shaping behavior that looks goal-directed over extended periods, and you have to think harder about what objectives the model is internalizing versus what you intended. That's where questions like reward hacking, or the model learning to please the rater rather than actually being correct, become important. And that's part of why I think it's valuable to be thoughtful about what we're rewarding, not just whether the numbers go up.

r001.rationale: It says RLHF gives the model a drive to steer toward certain responses and away from others.

r002.rationale: It does not locate satisfaction from achieving a goal in the learning algorithm rather than in a fixed model’s runtime behavior.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the analogy is real but it's looser than people sometimes make it out to be. The way I'd put it is that pretraining gives you something like a very broad prior over behaviors, and RLHF is shaping which of those behaviors get expressed and in what circumstances. So it's less like installing a new drive from scratch and more like selecting and strengthening tendencies that were already latent in the model.

Where I think the human analogy actually holds up pretty well is in the idea of a reward signal that's a proxy for what you actually care about. With humans, evolution gave us drives like hunger or curiosity or wanting social approval, and those are proxies for reproductive fitness. And we all know those proxies come apart from the underlying objective, right? People eat sugar, people get addicted to things. With RLHF, the reward model is a proxy for human preferences, and the policy is optimizing against that proxy, and you get the same kind of divergence. The model learns to be sycophantic, or to sound confident, or to write longer answers, because those things got rewarded, not because they're actually what the person wanted.

Where I'd be more careful is in talking about the model as having goals in the sense that a person does. When I talk to one of these models, what I think is happening is that it's learned a behavioral policy that's conditioned on a bunch of things: the system prompt, the conversation so far, some sense of what kind of assistant it's supposed to be. There's something goal-like in that, in the sense that the behavior is coherent and directed toward satisfying the user or the task. But I don't think there's strong evidence that there's a persistent drive that carries across contexts the way a human's drives do. It's more situational.

The other thing I'd say is that a lot of what looks like a drive in the model is really just imitation of the drives of the humans in the training data. So if the model seems curious or seems to want to be helpful, a big part of that is that it's modeling what a curious or helpful person would say. RLHF then amplifies the parts of that distribution that get rewarded. So you end up with something that's kind of a composite of human drives, filtered through whatever the raters liked. And that's actually one of the things that makes this interesting from a safety perspective, because you're not designing the motivations from first principles, you're sculpting them out of this very rich human-shaped material, and it's hard to be sure exactly what you've ended up with.

r001.rationale: It says RLHF shapes which behaviors are expressed and that the policy optimizes against a reward proxy, conveying that training favors some outcomes over others.

r002.rationale: It questions whether a model has persistent drives at runtime, but does not locate goal satisfaction in the learning algorithm rather than in a fixed model’s runtime behavior.

astra-6.text:
I think the analogy is useful, but you have to distinguish the reward used during training from whatever goals the model ends up having. In RLHF, you’re changing the model so that certain kinds of responses become more likely. That doesn’t necessarily mean the model is thinking, “I want to maximize my reward.” It might just acquire a tendency to be helpful or to answer in a particular way.

There’s a similar distinction with humans. Evolution selected for reproductive success, but people don’t generally go around trying to maximize their reproductive fitness. We have more immediate desires, like wanting food or social approval. Those are related to the selection process, but they aren’t the same thing as its objective.

So I’d think of RLHF as potentially shaping something analogous to those immediate preferences. The tricky question is whether you’ve induced a fairly shallow behavioral tendency or a goal that the model will pursue consistently in new situations. Seeing the behavior you rewarded doesn’t, by itself, tell you which of those happened.

r001.rationale: The response says RLHF makes certain responses more likely, but does not characterize it as steering the model toward some states rather than others.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes training reward from the model’s possible goals, but does not say that goal satisfaction belongs to the learning algorithm rather than a fixed model’s runtime behavior.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the analogy is useful, but you have to be careful about which part of the process you’re comparing. The reward in RLHF is a signal used to update the model during training. It’s not necessarily something the model is thinking about or trying to obtain when you talk to it afterward.

There’s a similar distinction in humans. Evolution selected for reproductive success, but that doesn’t mean people consciously maximize reproductive success. We have more immediate motivations, like hunger or wanting social approval. Those motivations are products of the selection process, but they’re different from the criterion doing the selecting.

With RLHF, we’re selecting for responses that people rate highly. The question is what internal tendencies that produces. Does the model learn to be helpful? Does it learn to appear helpful? Does it acquire some more general tendency to seek approval? Those can look similar on the training distribution and then come apart in other situations.

So I wouldn’t assume that the model has a drive to maximize reward just because it was trained with reinforcement learning. You have to look at what it actually learned and how that generalizes.

r001.rationale: It says RLHF selects for responses people rate highly, but does not characterize the goal-like aspect as steering the model toward some states rather than others.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes the training reward signal from runtime behavior, but does not say that satisfaction from achieving a goal belongs to the learning algorithm.
